---
title: "Data preparation"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every component of the package reads one prepared object, made once by
`pp_data()` from a data frame and the names of its columns. This page
explains what the object records and the decisions it embodies.

## The unit of observation

A row of the data is one **observation**: whatever the measure counts
outcomes on.

| Unit | Example | Outcome per row |
|---|---|---|
| patient-month | one row per patient per calendar month | 0/1 (an event in the month), or a count of days out of the days at risk |
| index discharge | one row per hospital discharge | 0/1 (readmitted within 30 days) |
| patient-record | one row per patient per provider per year | a time at risk and an event indicator |
| patient | one row per patient | a continuous value |

A patient usually contributes several rows, and those rows are **not
independent**: a patient sicker than the risk factors say is sicker in
every month. `pp_data()` therefore takes the patient identifier as well as
the provider identifier. The patient column is what the patient-clustered
(robust and stabilized) tests need; without it only the naive tests are
available.

## Declaring the columns

```{r}
library(pprof)
d <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 30, seed = 1)
str(d)
pd <- pp_data(d, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", cutoff = 10)
```

* `y`: the outcome. Binary (0/1), binomial (the number of events out of the
  `n` trials of the row, for instance hospital days out of days at risk) or
  continuous; `outcome = "auto"` tells them apart, and `outcome` can be
  given explicitly.
* `x`: the risk factors, numeric. Code a factor as 0/1 columns first (the
  package does not expand factors, so that the design matrix is exactly
  what you declared).
* `provider`, `patient`: identifiers, converted to character.
* `n`: the trials column of a binomial outcome.

### Survival outcomes

A time-to-event outcome is given by its at-risk interval and event
indicator instead of `y`:

```{r}
s <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 30, type = "survival", seed = 1)
head(s)
ps <- pp_data(s, x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider", patient = "patient",
              time = "stop", start = "start", event = "event", cutoff = 0)
```

`time` is the end of the interval, `start` its beginning (0 when absent:
no left truncation), `event` 0/1. A patient's follow-up may be cut into
several rows (counting-process form), for instance one per calendar year or
one per provider the patient was attributed to. Two more columns are read
by the Cox model only: `weights` (case weights) and `offset` (a known term
of the linear predictor).

## What `pp_data()` records

```{r}
pd
head(pd$sizes)
pd$vars
```

* `data`: the named columns, sorted by provider and then patient. The sort
  is stable and in the C locale, so a patient's rows keep their input
  order; sort by time within patient beforehand when the stabilized
  variance will be used.
* `sizes`: one row per provider with its number of rows and patients, and
  three flags: `included`, `no_events`, `all_events`.
* `vars`: the column names and the outcome type, which every later function
  reads, so that nothing is declared twice.

## The cutoff

Providers with fewer than `cutoff` patients (rows, when there is no patient
column) are kept in the data with `included = FALSE` and left out of model
fitting: too little information to estimate an effect, and in the measures
such providers are reported as "too few patients". The comparison is `>=`
on the number of patients.

For the two-stage survival models the convention is different: every
provider enters the stratified fit (`cutoff = 0`) and the providers to
report are chosen at the test stage (`test(fit, min_expected = 3)` and the
`providers` argument).

## Providers whose outcomes are all the same

A provider with no events, or with an event in every row, has no finite
maximum-likelihood effect: `no_events` and `all_events` mark them. Such
providers are fitted at the bound of the parameter space (`bound` in
`fit_logistic_fe()`, 10 on the logit scale around the median), they can be
tested with the score or exact statistic but not with the Wald statistic,
and the Firth penalty (`fit_logistic_fe(penalty = "firth")`) gives them a
finite estimate.

## Checks

`pp_check()` runs first (`check = TRUE`): missing values in the named
columns and constant risk factors are errors; near-constant risk factors,
pairs of risk factors with correlation above 0.9 and variance inflation
factors above 10 are warnings. It can be called on its own with other
thresholds:

```{r}
pp_check(d, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider", cor_threshold = 0.8)
```

## Simulated data

`sim_kecc()` simulates data of every outcome type with the structure of the
measures: patients nested in providers, several rows per patient, a
provider effect, a patient random effect that makes a patient's rows
correlated, and a few risk factors. The true parameters are kept in
`attr(d, "truth")`. The articles use it throughout; replace it with your
data frame.
